name: Tilly and the Snowbound Express
description: Winter comes to the night train, and Marigold gets gently stuck in the snow. Luckily, a hedgehog, a bear and a very large pot of cocoa are on board.

chapters.title: The First Snow
text: On the first night of winter, the little blue-and-pink train named Marigold left Hollow Station a quarter of an hour late. It was not her fault. The snow had come down all afternoon in great soft flakes, and the platform was so thick with it that the stationmaster had to dig the signal lamp out with a spoon.

Tilly the hedgehog was wearing three scarves and a woolly hat with a bobble. She stood at the door of the first carriage, punching tickets with a very small, very cold punch. "Mind the step," she said. "It is a bit slippery. Everything is a bit slippery."

The passengers climbed aboard, stamping and sniffing. There was the bear in the nightcap, with a pillow and a flask. There were the two rabbits and their one umbrella, which was no use at all in snow, but which they refused to leave behind. And there was the owl, with her lantern and her thick book, and a little tin of ginger biscuits.
"Chuff," said Marigold, quietly, and began to roll. The snowflakes swirled past the windows, silver and slow. Nobody minded the delay. A snowy night is the best kind of night to be on a train.

chapters.title: Marigold Slows Down
text: The snow grew deeper as the night went on. Marigold puffed along, slower and slower, her wheels crunching softly in the white. "Chuff," she said, then, "chuff," then, after a long pause, "chuff."

Tilly walked down the carriage with her tray of warm milk. "Marigold is being very brave," she told the passengers. "But the snow is deep, and I think she might need a rest." The bear nodded wisely and took a biscuit. "Resting is a perfectly good plan," he said.

At the top of a long, gentle hill, Marigold gave a small, apologetic sigh, and stopped. She was not stuck, exactly. She was only resting. But when the conductor, a calm and very tall heron, stepped out to look, the snow was up past the first step, and glowing faintly blue in the dark.
"We shall wait for the plough," said the heron, with great dignity. "It will come at dawn. In the meantime, I suggest we make ourselves at home."

chapters.title: The Cocoa Plan
text: Making oneself at home on a stopped train is a special skill, and the bear turned out to be very good at it. He fluffed his pillow, rolled up his sleeves and produced, from somewhere in his coat, an enormous pot, a ladle and a bag of chocolate.

"Cocoa," he said, simply. "It is the answer to most things." The rabbits found a small stove at the back of the carriage. The owl produced a block of butter and a spoon. Tilly, who knew where everything was, brought cups for everyone, and a jar of honey, and a very small sprig of mint.

Soon the whole carriage smelled of chocolate. The windows fogged up, and the lamp glowed gold, and the snow outside seemed not so much cold as cozy, a great white blanket tucked around the train. The cocoa was dark and creamy, and the bear stirred it with enormous care, in slow, wide circles, humming.
By the time the first cup was poured, even the conductor had taken off his hat. "Well," he said, taking a sip, "this is the best delay I have ever had."

chapters.title: Stories by the Stove
text: One by one, the passengers gathered around the little stove. The owl opened her thick book and read aloud, in a low, slow voice, about a lighthouse that learned to sing. The rabbits listened with their ears folded down. The bear listened with his eyes closed, though he insisted he was not asleep.

When the owl finished, the heron told a story about the first train that ever crossed the Silver Bridge, and how it was so nervous that it whistled the wrong note, and the bridge, being polite, whistled the same wrong note back, and so it became the right one.

Tilly told the last story. It was short, and about a hedgehog who got very cold, and very sleepy, and was given a cup of cocoa by a friend. "And that," said Tilly, "was the whole story. Nothing else happened. It was perfect."
Everyone agreed. Outside, the snow kept falling, and the lamp burned steady, and the carriage was so warm that one of the rabbits fell asleep in her cup.

chapters.title: The Plough at Dawn
text: The plough arrived at first light, a great, patient machine with a big, round, cheerful lamp. It pushed the snow aside in a long, white wave, and Marigold, who had been dozing, woke up with a start. "Oh!" she said. "Am I late?" "Only a little," said Tilly, patting her side. "And you were wonderful."

The sky was pink and gold. The snow sparkled like sugar. The passengers stepped out onto the platform one by one, stretching, yawning and smiling. The bear carried his pillow and an empty pot. The owl carried her book, and, tucked inside, a pressed snowflake that had come in through the window.

"Thank you," said the rabbits to Marigold, and bowed. "Thank you," said the owl, and the bear, and the heron. Marigold, who was not used to being thanked so much, blushed a deep, rosy pink all the way along her boiler.

Tilly climbed into the luggage rack, which was still warm, and curled into a ball. "Good morning, Marigold," she whispered. And the little train, in the first pale light, gave one long, contented puff, and let the winter settle around her, soft and white and kind.
